---
title: "Making work easier to review"
last-reviewed: "2026-08-28"
---

“Any thoughts?” is an easy message to send with a draft. It leaves your reviewer with a harder job: working out whether you want help with the argument, the analysis or the wording.

Give them a short cover note. Say what stage the draft has reached, what you need help deciding and when you need a response. Then, when comments come back, work out the concern behind each one before choosing a revision. You can use advice carefully without following every suggested edit.

## Ask for the review you need {#tell-the-reviewer-what-decision-the-draft-must-support}

Tell the reviewer who the draft is for, what you have checked and what is still unfinished. Agree a realistic response window, especially when another task depends on it.

You remain responsible for understanding the revised argument. Ask about advice you cannot yet explain, and respect decisions that belong to formal review or approval processes.

## Choose the review level

| Level | Useful question | Material to provide | Usually premature |
|---|---|---|---|
| Direction | Is this the right question, contribution or route? | one-page case, options and recommendation | sentence editing |
| Argument | Does the reasoning support the claim? | argument map and representative evidence | formatting polish |
| Structure | Can the reader follow the chapter's jobs and sequence? | full skeleton or developmental draft | isolated word choice |
| Method or analysis | Is the design, implementation or inference defensible? | protocol, code/output, deviations and exact questions | broad “thoughts?” request |
| Reporting | Is the account complete, accurate and bounded? | substantive draft and reporting checks | cosmetic refinement |
| Copy and production | Is the final expression and package correct? | stable near-final version | major conceptual redesign |

Choose the level that would help most now. A full review across every level needs the reviewer's agreement and enough time.

## Add a short cover note {#create-a-review-contract}

Before sending a substantial draft, agree or state:

- exact file, version and authoritative location;
- purpose and intended reader;
- draft maturity;
- the decision the review should support;
- one to three priority questions;
- checks already completed;
- known gaps and material excluded from review;
- expected depth and format of response;
- realistic review window and decision date; and
- where responses and decisions will be recorded.

::: {.decision-card}
**Smallest useful next action:** Add a cover note that lets a busy reviewer understand the decision, state and requested response without first reading the entire draft.
:::

If timing matters, ask before sending a large package. “Can you review a 9,000-word full chapter for argument and structure by 18 September?” is a request that can be accepted, renegotiated or declined. “Please send feedback soon” hides the dependency.

## Make it easy to see what changed

A reviewable package should allow the reader to:

1. identify what changed since the last version;
2. navigate to the consequential sections;
3. trace important claims to sources or outputs;
4. distinguish stable content from provisional markers;
5. see unresolved decisions and constraints;
6. comment without creating competing authoritative copies; and
7. know what response will count as complete.

Use stable headings, line numbers or section identifiers. For code or analysis, include the input state, exact command or notebook, expected output and failing test. For a design decision, provide the options and their trade-offs alongside your recommendation.

## Diagnose vague feedback

Translate the wording into a testable underlying issue:

| Comment | Possible underlying issue | Clarifying question |
|---|---|---|
| “Be more critical” | sources are summarised but not compared; warrants or contrary evidence are missing | Which claim most needs comparison or challenge? |
| “Needs more literature” | central claim lacks support, a field is missing or the boundary is unclear | Which decision or claim is currently unsupported? |
| “This doesn't flow” | paragraph functions, order or transitions are unclear | Where did the argument become difficult to follow? |
| “Do more analysis” | uncertainty or alternative explanation remains unresolved | What inference would the proposed analysis change? |
| “Simplify” | scope, terminology or sentence load exceeds the reader's need | Which idea or audience should govern the simplification? |

If a comment would change the argument or method and you are unsure what it means, paraphrase your understanding and ask the reviewer to check it.

## Process feedback in a response matrix

For each substantive comment:

1. preserve the comment or a faithful summary;
2. identify the underlying concern;
3. classify it as accept, adapt, investigate, discuss or decline;
4. state the proposed response and rationale;
5. link the changed location or evidence;
6. identify effects elsewhere in the project; and
7. mark completion only after verification.

Comments can reveal a real problem while suggesting the wrong solution. “Add 20 citations” may signal that a central claim is ungrounded; narrowing the claim and adding three directly relevant sources may be a better response. Record why.

## Resolve conflicting feedback

When reviewers disagree:

1. state each recommendation faithfully;
2. identify whether they answer the same question and assume the same audience;
3. locate the actual decision and its owner;
4. compare options against contribution, evidence, method, genre, feasibility and formal requirements;
5. propose a resolution;
6. ask reviewers to discuss the unresolved decision together where useful; and
7. record the decision and downstream changes.

Do not silently implement the last or most senior comment merely to end discomfort. Do not triangulate supervisors through separate messages. If the disagreement concerns safety, integrity, approvals, authorship, discrimination or supervision breakdown, use independent specialist or formal support.

## Example: “rewrite the discussion”

A student sends a 4,200-word discussion with “Could you give feedback?” One supervisor asks for a stronger practical recommendation. Another asks for a rewrite because the design cannot support that recommendation.

The study is cross-sectional, the outcome is self-reported and subgroup estimates are imprecise. Start by asking what implication that evidence supports. The student could remove the recommendation or present it as a hypothesis for prospective evaluation. Additional evidence from another study would help only if it supports the proposed action.

The student revises the causal language, separates association from mechanism and asks both supervisors whether the narrower implication resolves the disagreement. They then check the abstract and discussion together and link the changed passages in the response matrix. Any remaining objections stay in the decision record.

## Protect independence while using expertise

As you gain experience, practise using feedback to:

- diagnose the underlying problem;
- seek the right expertise;
- compare advice with evidence and requirements;
- propose and justify a response;
- implement it accurately; and
- explain the remaining uncertainty.

Supervisors remain responsible for their roles, and students should not be abandoned under the label of independence. Conversely, a reviewer rewriting every sentence can obscure whether the student understands the argument and can create attribution or authorship questions. Agree what kind of intervention is appropriate.

## When feedback is late

Record the agreed review window, its dependency and the decision date. Follow up with the exact material and requested decision. If delay threatens a milestone or repeats despite agreed arrangements, bring the record, impact, feasible alternatives and requested resolution to the appropriate supervision or graduate research process.

Keep the document marked as awaiting review until you receive a decision.

## Check the revision before sending it back

Work through substantive comments and record whether you accepted, adapted or declined the suggestion, with your reason. Revisit the concern after editing: did the change answer it? Check the abstract and other linked sections too.

Send one current version with a short account of the changes, known gaps and any unresolved questions. If the request or timing has changed, agree the next review with the reviewer. Use the cover-note template below to make the request specific without adding a long administrative exercise.

## Sources and limits

The review levels and response matrix are editorial suggestions. The distinction among goals, current performance and actionable next steps is informed by broader educational feedback research, whose effects are heterogeneous and not doctorate-specific [@hattie-timperley-2007; @wisniewski2020feedback].
